1. Core Clinical Tension: A 38-year-old female presented with a 5-month history of progressive spastic dysarthria, dysphagia, nasal regurgitation, and emotional lability (pseudobulbar palsy), combined with focal motor seizures and left upper-extremity weakness. This constellation of upper motor neuron bulbar signs and asymmetric limb weakness closely mimicked primary neurodegenerative motor neuron disease (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis) or high-grade intracerebral glioma, rather than an intracranial parasitic infection.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission clinical encounter concludes following clinical neurologic examination and baseline triage laboratory studies (normal peripheral smear, renal panel, and liver function tests), immediately prior to brain MRI and targeted neurocysticercosis serology.
3. Differential Distinctions: Motor neuron disease (ALS with bulbar onset) was considered due to spastic dysarthria, hyperactive jaw jerk, and limb weakness, but was argued against by absence of fasciculations/atrophy, cortical sensory loss, and focal seizures. Brain neoplasm (high-grade glioma) was considered for focal seizures and unilateral paresis, but excluded by MRI findings. Confirmation of neurocysticercosis was established by brain MRI demonstrating multiple bihemispheric cysts with mural scolex (vesicular stage) alongside a giant intraparenchymal cyst, supported by positive parasite serology.
case_prompt:
A 38-year-old woman presented with progressive dysarthria, dysphagia, nasal regurgitation, and hypernasal speech of 5 months' duration. During this same 5-month period, she experienced 4 episodes of focal seizures involving the right upper and lower extremities, for which she had not received antiepileptic medications. Over the preceding 15 days, she noticed new weakness in her left upper extremity. She also exhibited emotional lability characterized by unprovoked episodes of crying. She reported no headaches, vomiting, or visual blurring.

On neurological examination, she demonstrated spastic dysarthria with exaggerated jaw jerks and a hyperactive gag reflex. Motor testing revealed both proximal and distal weakness in the left upper extremity with a muscle power of 3/5. Deep tendon reflexes were brisk throughout, with bilaterally mute plantar responses. Sensory testing demonstrated cortical sensory loss in the left upper extremity. There was no muscular atrophy or fasciculations. Funduscopic examination and general systemic examinations were normal.

Baseline laboratory investigations showed a normal peripheral blood smear, and normal serum renal and liver function parameters.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Motor neuron disease / Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (bulbar onset)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to the progressive subacute onset of spastic dysarthria, dysphagia, exaggerated jaw jerk/gag reflex, and asymmetric upper extremity weakness; ruled out by absence of muscle atrophy and fasciculations, presence of focal motor seizures, cortical sensory loss, and cystic neuroimaging.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Neurological examination showed exaggerated jaw jerks and gag reflex with spastic dysarthria... There was no atrophy or fasciculation of the affected muscles.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to focal seizures, progressive hemiparesis (left upper limb power 3/5), and cortical sensory signs indicative of a focal expanding cerebral hemispheric lesion; ruled out by MRI demonstrating multiple discrete cysts containing scoleces rather than an infiltrating neoplastic mass.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: She had 4 episodes of partial seizures involving the right upper and the lower limb for the past 5 months and was not on any medications. There was weakness of the left upper limb for the past 15 days duration... The MRI brain showed multiple small cysts with scolex in both the cerebral hemispheres and a giant intraparenchymal cyst measuring 5 x 4.3 cms in the right cerebral hemisphere [Figure 1a and b].

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Brain MRI demonstrated pathognomonic multiple small parenchymal cysts with visible scolex in both cerebral hemispheres and a giant intraparenchymal cyst (5 x 4.3 cm) in the right hemisphere in the vesicular stage, corroborated by positive neurocysticercosis serology, resulting in rapid symptom resolution following albendazole and corticosteroid therapy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The MRI brain showed multiple small cysts with scolex in both the cerebral hemispheres and a giant intraparenchymal cyst measuring 5 x 4.3 cms in the right cerebral hemisphere [Figure 1a and b]... Her NCC serology was positive and diagnosis confirmed by MRI, which showed multiple cysts with scolex (in vesicular stage).

editor_comments: Presentation of neurocysticercosis with pseudobulbar palsy is exceptionally rare, usually caused by bilateral opercular or corticobulbar tract lesions. Neuroimaging showing the pathognomonic scolex inside cysts confirms the diagnosis.
